facts.text: Tosca premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome on 14 January 1900, a day late, because of fears of unrest.
evidence: It premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome on 14 January 1900.
its first performance was delayed for a day for fear of disturbances

facts.text: Police had warnings of an anarchist bomb at the premiere. The conductor, Mugnone, was told to strike up the royal march in an emergency.
facts.evidence: Police received warnings of an anarchist bombing of the theatre, and instructed Mugnone

facts.text: The critics were lukewarm, but the public loved it: the premiere was followed by twenty performances, all to packed houses.
evidence: Much of the critical and press reaction was lukewarm
the premiere was followed by twenty performances, all given to packed houses

facts.text: Puccini begged his publisher in 1889 to get Sardou’s permission: “I see in this Tosca the opera I need, with no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle.”
facts.attribution: Puccini, letter to Giulio Ricordi, 7 May 1889 (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: I see in this Tosca the opera I need, with no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle

facts.text: The young Enrico Caruso hoped to create Cavaradossi but was passed over for the more experienced Emilio De Marchi.
facts.evidence: The young Enrico Caruso had hoped to create the role of Cavaradossi, but was passed over in favour of the more experienced Emilio De Marchi.

facts.text: There is no prelude: the opening chords are Scarpia’s motif, and Angelotti bursts straight in.
facts.evidence: The opera begins without any prelude; the opening chords of the Scarpia motif lead immediately to the agitated appearance of Angelotti

facts.text: As the Te Deum procession fills the church, Scarpia joins the prayer: “Tosca, you make me forget even God!”
facts.evidence: Tosca, you make me forget even God!

facts.text: Maria Jeritza, said to be Puccini’s favorite Tosca, once fell while escaping Scarpia and sang “Vissi d’arte” lying on the floor. It was such a success that she kept doing it.
evidence: was said to be Puccini's favorite Tosca
Jeritza was the first to deliver "Vissi d'arte" from a prone position, having fallen to the stage while eluding the grasp of Scarpia.
Jeritza sang the aria while on the floor thereafter

facts.text: For the Roman dawn, Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear the matins bells, and had bells cast by four different foundries.
evidence: went to the Castel Sant'Angelo to measure the sound of matins bells there
Puccini had bells for the Roman dawn cast to order by four different foundries.

facts.text: Librettist Illica grumbled after the premiere that all the fuss and money spent on the bells “passes completely unnoticed”.
facts.attribution: Luigi Illica, letter to Ricordi (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: the great fuss and the large amount of money for the bells have constituted an additional folly, because it passes completely unnoticed

facts.text: The shepherd boy’s song is in Roman dialect. Puccini asked for a “good romanesco poet”, and folklorist Giggi Zanazzo wrote the verse.
evidence: The composer asked a friend to have a "good romanesco poet" write some words

facts.text: Ricordi noticed that part of “O dolci mani” was borrowed from music Puccini had cut from his early opera Edgar, and demanded changes. There wasn’t time.
evidence: some of the music for Cavaradossi's act 3 aria, "O dolci mani" was borrowed from music Puccini had cut from his early opera, Edgar
time was too short before the scheduled January 1900 premiere to make any further changes

facts.text: In the 1950s musicologist Joseph Kerman called Tosca a “shabby little shocker”. Conductor Thomas Beecham replied that anything Kerman says about Puccini “can safely be ignored”.
evidence: described Tosca as a "shabby little shocker."

facts.text: The Met premiere was on 4 February 1901, only a year after the world premiere.
facts.evidence: The premiere at the Metropolitan Opera was on 4 February 1901

facts.text: Luciano Pavarotti’s last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.
facts.evidence: Pavarotti's last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.

facts.text: Sardou’s play La Tosca, written for Sarah Bernhardt, had more than 3,000 performances in France alone.
facts.evidence: with more than 3,000 performances in France alone

facts.text: By cutting several numbers, Puccini left “three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama”, as his biographer put it.
facts.attribution: Mary Jane Phillips-Matz, Puccini biography (via Wikipedia)
facts.evidence: leaving three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama
